local_precedent.text: Present-day flood pathways into the study area were identified at Tenean Beach/Conley Street, southeast of Kosciuszko Circle, Bianculli Boulevard, Pattens Cove, and Quincy Shore Drive/Neponset Trail; in a 2030 extreme event these expand and new pathways appear from Moakley Park and the I-93 underpass.
The study notes flood protection is being advanced outside the central section (Bianculli Boulevard to Freeport Street), leaving that area as a key storm-surge pathway into the study area.
The study records that DCR's 2017 Morrissey Boulevard redesign planned to elevate the roadway for coastal resiliency, with a stated target of limiting tidal-flooding closures to fewer than 3 in 2065.

Stormwater flooding may remain a significant problem in the Central section because of limited gravity discharge at high tide; one option assumes BWSC's proposed additional stormwater infrastructure for the Northern section.

Key findings state flood mitigation could be implemented along the coastline and Dorchester Bay Basin, should focus on nature-based solutions, and that environmental permitting is expected to be complex.
Infrastructure in the area is owned by multiple jurisdictions (including MassDOT, DCR, MBTA, City of Boston, utilities, and private owners), so any project needs coordinated ownership and permitting.

blocks.text: Flooding on this corridor is documented or modelled, and drainage complaints are reported nearby. The cause is not established. Possible explanations: coastal overtopping / overland inflow, high tide blocking stormwater discharge / backflow, localized inlet obstruction / debris.
The road is where flooding is seen. The asset that needs work may be an inlet, pipe, outfall, or shoreline opening elsewhere in the system.
Possibly coastal overtopping / overland inflow (possible). Evidence is consistent with this cause but does not establish it.
Supports: [published model] MC-FRM 2050, 1% annual exceedance (projected): 23 of 31 corridor roads exposed; depth not available / requires site survey.
Supports: [observed measurement] January 4, 2018 nor'easter (USGS observed peak footprint): 10 of 31 corridor roads exposed; depth not available / requires site survey.
Does not prove it: A flood polygon over the road does not show where water enters at road scale.
Missing: Shoreline / edge elevations along the pathway (survey, vertical datum); Which opening or low point admits the water.
Possibly high tide blocking stormwater discharge / backflow (possible). Evidence is consistent with this cause but does not establish it.

Supports: [published model] Stormwater flooding may remain a significant problem in the Central section because of limited gravity discharge at high tide; one option assumes BWSC's proposed additional stormwater infrastructure for the Northern section.
Does not prove it: High tide alone does not show that a specific outfall is failing.
Missing: Which outfall(s) serve the corridor inlets and who owns them; Outfall invert elevations vs tide levels (datum).

Supports: [observed report] 1 311 report(s) at INTERSECTION of Norwood St & William T Morrissey Blvd  Dorchester  MA (Catchbasin: 1), 2018-01-12 to 2018-01-12, 3 m from corridor.

Multiple simultaneous causes / unresolved: possible. 3 mechanisms have some supporting evidence; the evidence does not discriminate between them.

Next checks: Survey the shoreline edge and suspected entry pathway; Trace corridor inlets to their outfall(s) and confirm owner; Compare reported flooding dates against tide and rainfall records; Inspect and, if blocked, clean the corridor catch basins; CCTV the connecting pipe if cleaning does not restore drainage; Convene asset owners and collect drainage records before choosing a measure; Drainage capacity assessment (inlets and pipes) with the owner's records; Topographic survey of gutters, low points and inlet positions.

Candidate to investigate: Raise the roadway profile (raised roadway barrier). Raise the road (and usually sidewalks) so the road itself acts as a flood barrier and/or stays above design flood elevation.
Cause check: Only relevant if coastal_overland is confirmed; currently possible.
The guideline sample considers raised roadways with a 4-ft grade change, and notes the approach may also apply to elevating emergency evacuation routes.
Option 1 (retaining walls and/or slopes) may be feasible where buildings are set back at least 14 ft from the back of sidewalk.
The guidelines do not recommend a raised roadway barrier where existing buildings sit at the back of sidewalk; raising only the roadway creates safety, drainage, ADA and access impacts.
Once a street is raised, a stormwater pump system (pumps, generators) adds ongoing O&M cost; the guideline expects stormwater costs to be significant, citing Miami Beach raised-road projects.
Raising one corridor does not by itself block flood pathways that enter around its ends or through adjacent low ground.
Needed before screening further: Building setbacks from back of sidewalk; Surveyed road elevation with vertical datum; Underground utilities; Drainage capacity, outfalls, tide gates.
Ways it could fail: Flanking around the ends of the raised section; Ponding behind the raised road without pumped drainage; Utility relocation conflicts; Driveway / building access grade conflicts.
